 Albemarle School Board launches first phase of 30-60-90 day plan to address crises
 The plan was presented by Acting Superintendent Dr. Chandra Hayes at Thursday's meeting, just three weeks after the board moved for her to draft it.
 By Jackson Hephner November 16, 2026 2:53 pm 
 Facebook 
 X 
 More 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 SMS 
 Cville Right Now Jay Hart ACPS Acting Superintendent Dr. Chandra Hayes 
 CHARLOTTESVILLE, VA ( CVILLE RIGHT NOW ) – Albemarle County’s School Board is launching the first phase of its 30-60-90 plan drafted by Acting Superintendent Dr. Chandra Hayes to address concerns that have arisen during the division’s recent crises. The board unanimously approved the plan, which sets benchmark achievements for the division to reach in 30 days, another set in 60 days, and then a final set in 90 days, at its Thursday meeting. 
 T he board directed Hayes to develop the plan during its Oct. 23 meeting. It will include the establishment of the division’s new Office of Compliance and Constituent Services as well as a whistleblower reporting system and an ongoing internal audit function.
 “This is not simply a 90-day response to current events,” Hayes said. “And it certainly should not be viewed as a checklist that we complete, put on a shelf, and consider our work finished. This plan represents the beginning of something much more important — building a sustainable system of compliance, transparency, and accountability within Albemarle County Public Schools.”
 The board moved for Hayes to draft this plan just days before Virginia Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway informed the division it would be initiating an independent review of ACPS’s “policies, practice and culture,” according to a letter sent by Conway to hayes and the School Board on Oct. 27. 
 Since then, Hayes said she and School Board Chair and White Hall representative Dr. Rebecca Berlin have already met with the VDOE three times. Hayes submitted the scope of work for the review to the department on Nov. 5 and has since received approval from the department.
 “In a way, the work that the (Virginia Department of Education) is asking us to do and that we want and need to do is almost the starting point for it,” Berlin told Cville Right Now earlier this month. “And then this Office of Compliance and Constituent services will continue that work now and in the future.” 
 In the first 30 days, the division will “establish the foundation,” by seeking approval of its selected contractor and scope of work from the VDOE, posting the search for a Director of Compliance and Constituent Services, or DOCCS, and inventorying current reporting processes, Hayes said.
 The next phase will focus on “building the structure,” conducting interviews for the DOCCS position and implementing the whistleblower system, as well as establishing mandated CPS tracking, training completion checks, written procedures and a corrective action log. 
 Berlin explained earlier this month that part of the job of the Office of Compliance and Constituent Services will be to modernize ACPS’s data and establish a centralized system, making it easier to monitor metrics and fulfill FOIA requests.
 “We don’t have what I would just say are 21st century data systems,” she said. “We’re tracking all that data, but we’re tracking it in a way through Excel Spreadsheets and other types of documents that you can’t, that aren’t easily searchable individually, as well as across pieces of information.”
 The final 30 days will focus on reporting the evidence, taking “necessary board action,” Hayes said, and establishing practices that will continue beyond the 90 days. This phase will also include a reorganization plan presented to the board, the delivery of an interim report to ACPS and VDOE, the hiring of a director and coordinator for the Office of Compliance and Constituent Services, and the first quarterly compliance report. 
 The division will also be adopting a charter for an ongoing internal audit function, administered by the DOCCS. The selected contractor will begin its work with an organizational study, and they will report to the Board through a Board Audit Committee. Future work will be through an annual audit plan the board approves. While the DOCCS will administer the contract, the auditor will maintain its independence in its methods and conclusions.
 “The expectation will be ongoing independent reviews rather than one-time assurances,” Hayes said.
 Hayes will present a report to the School Board at the end of each 30-day period. The first will be at the School Board’s Dec. 10 meeting. the second will be at its Jan. 14 meeting, and the third will be at its Feb. 11 meeting, assuming the proposed Board calendar for next year is approved.
 Beyond the 90-day period, the division will be expecting the final report from the independent review in April, and ACPS will continue working with the VDOE on implementation afterward. A risk-based annual audit plan is expected in May, and recurring costs will be included in the FY 2027-28 budget.
 The one-time cost of this plan is estimated to be $515,000. $240,000 will go toward the independent organizational study and the VDOE-required review, $200,000 will go toward establishing the Office of Compliance and Constituent Services, hiring its director and coordinator, and establishing its tracking systems, and the remaining $75,000 will go toward FOIA administrative support and contracted communication support. 
 Hayes said additional state revenue released after the FY 2026-27 budget was adopted as the proposed funding source for these costs. If those funds, or any others, need to be appropriated by board action, Hayes plans to make those requests at the Dec. 10 meeting.
 “Final system selections and their costs will be disclosed before funds are committed,” she said. “And recurring expenses will be considered in the next budget cycle.”
 As part of its approval, the board authorized Hayes to carry out the plan’s work. Any appropriations, policy actions, appointments, contractual approvals, and reorganization decisions will still need separate board actions when required.
 The plan was met with universal praise from the board, with multiple board members telling Hayes they have the board’s full support and ensuring her that if she finds that if ends up needing more resources down the road, she should feel comfortable coming to the board with those potential changes.
 “To accomplish this, we want to be able to give you what you need,” at-large member David Storm said. “So, this needs to be a living document in many ways. And if you get in 45 days and you think some of these things aren’t right anymore, you should feel comfortable coming back and telling us why and then explaining why you wanna move in a different direction and I think, because I think as you get into this, and as everybody else gets into this, this will change.” 
 Following the approval of the 30-60-90 plan, the School Board unanimously approved a vendor for the VDOE review and organizational review in a closed session. That vendor was not named publicly by the board.
